opening.headline: When performance is poor, learn how to determine the cause of failure and what to do first: prompt, search, or tuning.
body: Whether to write a longer prompt, add a search, or tune the model is a frequent debate on the team. The three methods have different costs and time, and if you choose the wrong one, you will end up with the same failure even if it takes a long time.

In this class, you will learn how to divide optimization into two axes: context and action, and classify failure cases into which of the two axes they fall into. First, we point out the structure that what the model knows comes from two places: weights and context. Next, we look at which problem prompt improvement, search improvement, and tuning are each levers to solve, and establish criteria for determining the most cost-effective order.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the two axes of optimization (context and action)
Failure cases can be classified into lack of context and behavior/format problems.
You can determine a cost-effective improvement path.
We can explain this by distinguishing between two sources of what the model knows: weights and context.
Explain the operating principle of RAG and tell how to evaluate the search phase and model phase separately.

screens.title: Performance is not working, what should I do first?
screens.lead: First, read about the situation of a team running an in-house document Q&A bot. As you read, think for yourself about which improvement plan fits the problem.

visual.alt: A scene where two failures of the Q&A bot and three candidates for improvement are placed side by side.
labels: What are the vacation rules this year?
The format is different every time

paragraphs: We have an in-house document Q&A bot. Some questions are answered using the old rules without knowing the latest rules that have changed this year. Also, in some questions, the content of the answer is correct, but the format is different each time, sometimes in a table and sometimes in lines.

The team's opinions are divided into three. One side says, “Let’s make the prompt longer,” another side says, “Let’s add a search,” and another side says, “Let’s tune the model.” All three have different costs and durations.

If you choose wrong, the same failure will remain even after weeks of use. For example, it's common to see cases where you've tuned the format to get it right, but the "don't know the latest information" problem remains. Conversely, solving the problem of unstable formats using the search function does not improve the problem.

So there is one key question this class asks. Is the cause of this failure due to lack of necessary information, or is the model's behavior inconsistent? If you can answer these questions, you can have a reason to decide which improvement plan to choose first.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Will “I don’t know the latest regulations” and “The format is jagged” be solved with the same prescription? After class, you will be able to answer this question with evidence.

screens.outro: Let me first think about whether you have had a similar experience.

screens.title: Think of similar scenes
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You will not enter or submit your answer, so think in your head first and then click.

items.prompt: When a model gives a wrong answer, have you ever wondered, “Did I get it wrong because I didn’t have the information, or did I do it wrong knowingly?”
items.answer: Since both cases appear to be “wrong answers” on the surface, it is easy to ignore them without distinguishing between them. However, if it is wrong due to lack of information, you can provide information, and if you did it knowingly and incorrectly, you must correct your behavior. If the cause is different, the treatment is also different.

items.prompt: Have you ever tried to refine a prompt only to find yourself stuck?
items.answer: This happens because there are problems that can be solved with prompts and problems that cannot be solved. If the required information is not in the input, the model cannot produce that information, no matter how elaborate the instructions. Feeling stuck can be a sign that the lever doesn't fit the problem.

items.prompt: Have you ever had the expectation that “fine-tuning will solve the problem”, but it was unclear what data was actually needed?
items.answer: Tuning is a method of learning behavior by showing many examples of desired input and output. So, if you don't know what behavior to learn and where to get the right examples, you can't get started. This class develops the ability to classify failures before tuning.

items.prompt: What do you want to gain from this class?
items.answer: In this class, we focus on gaining insight into two types of failure before choosing an improvement plan. By distinguishing between failures where information is lacking and failures where actions are unstable, we can naturally organize which problems each prompt, search, and tune are suited to.

screens.outro: Now, let's start by looking at the structure in which optimization consists of two axes.

screens.title: Optimization is a matrix of two axes, not one line
screens.lead: Select the number marker in the picture to see a detailed explanation. Check the markers one by one.

visual.alt: Illustration of a two-dimensional matrix with context optimization on the horizontal axis and LLM optimization on the vertical axis.

markers.label: Starting point: prompt
markers.title: The starting point is always a prompt and a baseline
markers.body: It all starts with writing and evaluating prompts to create a baseline. Starting with a simple prompt and expected output, we look at examples of errors, determine why they are wrong, and only then decide which lever to pull.

markers.label: Horizontal axis: context optimization
markers.title: Context Optimization: Increases Response Accuracy
markers.body: Pull this axis when the model needs knowledge that was not seen during training, when the knowledge is out of date, or when information that is private within the company is needed. This axis increases the accuracy of the response by adding necessary information to the model.

markers.label: Vertical axis: LLM optimization
markers.title: LLM Optimization: Increase Behavior Consistency
markers.body: This axis is pulled when the format of the results is jagged, the tone and writing style is off, or the reasoning process is not followed consistently. These are the axes that make the model behave consistently in the same way.

markers.label: moving path
markers.title: In reality, you move the grid around.
markers.body: Many guides speak of a straight sequence from prompt to RAG to tune, but in reality they are separate levers that solve different problems. It goes back and forth between the two axes, going through a cycle of evaluating, creating hypotheses, applying them, and evaluating them again.

screens.outro: Now that we have established the structure of the axes, let's look at where the model's knowledge comes from.

screens.title: Two sources of what the model knows: weights and context.
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to follow step by step where what the model knows comes from and when it changes.

visual.alt: A structural diagram showing that the model's knowledge comes from two sources: the weights solidified through learning and the context inserted when calling.
labels: The moment the model creates an answer
Subsequent events and internal documents are not included.

steps.title: The model's knowledge lies in its weights
steps.body: A language model is a function made up of many numbers, namely weights. In pre-learning, a large number of texts are shown, and the weights are repeatedly adjusted to match the next text given the previous text. In this process, grammar, common sense, and many facts are solidified into the weights, giving the model a “learned memory.”

steps.title: Weights stop after training
steps.body: The learned weights do not change each time a question is asked. Therefore, the model does not know what happened after the end of the data used for learning, or about in-house documents that were not included in the training data. This is why you answer with the previous regulations without knowing the changed vacation regulations this year. It's not that the model memorized it incorrectly; it's information that was never included in the weights in the first place.

steps.title: Even after pre-training, the weights are further modified.
steps.body: A model that has only completed pre-training may be good at continuing writing, but may be poor at following instructions. Therefore, additional steps such as supervised learning, which shows model responses written by humans, and preference learning, which shows the best response among multiple responses, are used to learn the behavior of following instructions well. As a representative example, the InstructGPT study showed a sequence of learning exemplar responses, ranking responses, and reinforcement learning with rankings as rewards (Ouyang et al., 2022). These steps are all about modifying the weights, and the tuning discussed in this class falls into this loop.

steps.title: Context is text entered as input when calling.
steps.body: Context is the entire input passed to the model in one call. Instructions, transcripts, examples, and references all go here. The model can read the instructions, examples, and data in the input and respond accordingly without changing the weights. The GPT-3 study demonstrated this ability by simply providing a prompt with a task description and a few examples and allowing the task to be performed without any need to fine-tune or update the model (Brown et al., 2020).

steps.title: Context has limits
steps.body: Information you put in the context is only used for that call and must be added again in the next call. There is also a limit to the length. Even if it is within the limit, research has reported that information placed in the middle of long input tends to be less utilized than information placed at the beginning or end (Liu et al., 2023). This is not to say that adding too much information is good, but that the necessary information must be included appropriately.

steps.title: Two sources become two axes
steps.body: To summarize, what the model knows comes from two places. Memories solidified by weights only change through learning and stop at the point of learning. The information in the context can be freely changed from call to call. Contextual optimization to add information involves changing the context, and behavioral optimization to make behavior consistent involves changing weights. The following screens apply this distinction to the failure case.

screens.outro: Now that we know the structure, let's try to determine which problem is responsible for one failed example.

ext.title: Ouyang et al. (2022), Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback
Brown et al. (2020), Language Models are Few-Shot Learners
Liu et al. (2023), Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts

screens.title: Divide failure cases into “look ups” and “learned memories”
screens.lead: Select the “Remember in Context” and “Learned Recall” buttons alternately to compare the differences between the two problems.

visual.alt: Illustration of the decision flow that classifies one incorrect assessment item into two types of memory problems.
labels: Did the input contain the facts needed for the answer?
Memory problems in context - Enter information (prompt, search)
Yes, but I wrote it wrong
Learned memory problems - teach by example (instructions, few shots, tuning)
The two methods can be stacked and used together

states.label: Memory in context (in-context)
states.body: It can be compared to opening a book and looking for it. This problem can be solved by entering the necessary information into the input when the model answers. There are two ways: There is a static method where you write directly into the prompt, and there is an industrial method, such as RAG, which searches for information that matches the question. Latest regulations or non-public information within the company that the model does not know are a problem here.

states.label: learned memory (learned)
states.body: It can be likened to learning by seeing the same type of case repeatedly over a long period of time. Solve this by showing examples of the desired input and the correct output for the given input and letting the model learn. Behaviors that must be consistently practiced every time, such as answer format, tone, and reasoning procedures, are the issues here.

screens.outro: Once the criteria for classification are established, we can look specifically at improving the first lever, the prompt.

screens.title: Improving Prompts: The Cheapest First Step
screens.lead: Select each tab to learn why improving your prompts is the first step, what techniques are available, and what's possible.

tabs.label: Why the first step
tabs.body: Prompt engineering is usually the best starting point. In some cases, such as summarization, translation, and code generation, practical accuracy and consistency can be achieved without examples. The biggest benefit is that it allows you to define for yourself what accuracy is. If you start with a simple prompt and expected output, when the results are different, the reasons will inform future improvements.

tabs.label: Techniques and Axes
tabs.body: Typical techniques include writing clear instructions, breaking complex tasks into subtasks, giving the model time to think, and systematically testing changes. Among these, providing reference texts and using external tools fall into the category of adding context. Clear instructions and time to think go a long way toward refining behavior. Breaking down subtasks and systematic testing helps on both axes.

tabs.label: Effect of few shot
tabs.body: A few-shot approach to teaching behavior is to show a few examples of correct input and output. In the Icelandic sentence correction case introduced in the document, the result was BLEU 62 without examples, but when few-shot examples were added, the result increased to 70. BLEU is an overlap metric that measures how much the output and reference sentences share consecutive word sets; higher values ​​mean they are more similar to the reference. This example shows that the model already has the necessary knowledge and only needs to refine its behavior.

tabs.label: limit
tabs.body: Prompts alone are difficult to scale. To handle a wider range of inputs, you need to dynamically add context to the input, and if more consistent behavior is needed, learning is necessary. An assessment set of at least 20 good prompts, questions, and baseline answers provides a baseline for moving on to the next step.

screens.outro: If prompts aren't enough, let's look at the representative lever of the context axis: search.

screens.title: Improved Search: Filling Context with RAG
screens.lead: By selecting and expanding each item, you can see what RAG is, where it fails, and how to improve it.

items.title: What is RAG
items.body: RAG is the process of augmenting a prompt with relevant content before generating an answer. It's a way to give models access to domain knowledge. Turn the knowledge base into an embedding, change the question to an embedding, find the closest content, and show it to the model. This way, even in-house documents that the model doesn't know about can be used in the answer. What embedding is and how to find nearby content is explained graphically in the following screen.

items.title: New axis: Search
items.body: The RAG app adds a new axis, search, to the existing two axes. So the number of places where failure occurs increases to two. You need to look at whether incorrect content was imported from the search stage or whether incorrect content was used during the model stage.

items.title: Failure of the search phase
items.body: If you give it the wrong context, the model won't be able to answer correctly. Conversely, if you provide too much irrelevant context, really needed information is buried and hallucinations increase. Having more context is not a good thing; it must be appropriate.

items.title: model step failure
items.body: This is a case where you receive the right context but do something wrong with it. In this case, improve the instructions first, and if correct examples are still helpful, consider tuning. In the end, we are trying to determine whether it is a search problem or a behavioral problem.

items.title: Search improvement direction
items.body: There are ways to adjust the search to produce relevant results, reduce noise, and increase the information contained in each result. In either case, the amount of improvement is confirmed by the evaluation set.

screens.outro: Now let's look at a representative lever on the behavioral axis: tuning.

screens.title: How RAG works and evaluating the search phase
screens.lead: If you select the number marker in the picture, each step of the RAG will be explained in detail. Check them one by one in numerical order, and see how the last two markers measure whether your search was successful.

visual.alt: A RAG flowchart in which the document is fragmented, embedded, and saved, fragments that are close to the question are found, inserted into the prompt, and the model answers.
labels: Embedding: Convert to list of numbers
Did you write the imported content properly?

markers.label: document into pieces
markers.title: Chunk: Split the document into reasonable sizes
markers.body: If you insert a long document as a whole, it is difficult to determine whether it is close to the question because multiple topics are mixed in one document, and the context limit is quickly filled. So we divide the document into chunks, each paragraph or section. If the piece is too small, the context is cut off and the meaning is lost. If the piece is too large, unnecessary information is mixed in. Fragment size is a control value that determines search quality.

markers.label: Embedding
markers.title: Embedding: Change words with similar meanings to numbers that are close to each other.
markers.body: Embedding is a way to turn text into a list of numbers. Words with similar meanings are created to be lists of numbers that are close together, so that "close" can be measured by distance, like dots on a map. So, you can find articles like “Vacation regulations” and “How to apply for annual leave” that have different words but are similar in meaning. Pre-embed all the pieces and put them in a searchable repository.

markers.label: Embedding questions as well
markers.title: Change the question in the same way to find the nearest piece
markers.body: When a question comes in, we embed it in the same way, finding the closest piece in the bin by distance. Get the top k items in closest order. k is a value that determines how many to retrieve. This step searches for close meaning, not whether the letters are the same, so you can find the word used in the question even if it is not in the document.

markers.label: Insert at prompt
markers.title: Put the imported fragment into context with a question
markers.body: You insert the imported fragment into the prompt with a question, and the model answers based on that content. RAG is a structure that adds information retrieved from external documents to the memory of a model solidified through learning (Lewis et al., 2020). If you change the document, the changed information will be used starting from the next question, so there is no need to retrain the model.

markers.label: Was the search correct?
markers.title: Search phase evaluation: Is the answer piece in the top k?
markers.body: Whether the search is successful can be measured separately from the model. For each question, we mark the fragment containing the answer in advance and count whether the fragment is in the top k. If the correct answer piece was in the top three for 41 out of 50 questions, the hit rate is 82% (hypothetical example). The remaining 9 are wrong because they have no basis, no matter how good the model is. If the hit rate is low, adjust the fragment size, embedding method, and k first.

markers.label: Did the model write well?
markers.title: Evaluate the model steps: Did you use what you imported correctly?
markers.body: If the search is correct but the answer is wrong, it is a problem at the model stage. You can separate the search and model by putting the answer fragment directly into the context and seeing if the answer is correct. Increasing k increases the hit rate, but it has also been reported that unrelated fragments may be included, burying necessary information, and information placed in the middle of long inputs may not be utilized well (Liu et al., 2023). So, we look at the hit rate and the accuracy of the answers together.

screens.outro: Now that we know why we separate the search and model phases, let's look at tuning, which is a lever on the behavioral axis.

ext.title: Lewis et al. (2020), Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
Liu et al. (2023), Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts

screens.title: Tuning: A lever for learning behavior
screens.lead: Hover over or select an underlined term to see an explanation. Check the terms one by one.

data.text: Tuning is a method of further training a model on a small domain dataset to solve the learned memory problem. The two main objectives are: first, to improve accuracy on specific tasks by exposing the model to many correctly performed examples; and second, to improve efficiency by achieving the same accuracy with fewer tokens or a smaller model. Replacing lengthy instructions and shot examples in prompts with training examples can reduce prompt tokens. Training examples must closely resemble actual service inputs and outputs. Research has also shown that responses can learn format and style from just a small number of high-quality examples. The LIMA study, which fine-tuned a model on 1,000 carefully selected prompt-response pairs, concluded that most of the model's knowledge comes from pre-training, while only a small amount of data is used to align the response format. The practice of compiling pilot service logs into a training set is referred to as prompt baking. After training is complete, the model is evaluated using a separate evaluation set set via overfitting. If the application involves search, the training examples must include the search context so that the model does not learn to answer without context.

terms.tip: This is a memory learned by repeating the same types of cases. It is about consistency of behavior, like form, tone, and reasoning procedures.
This method transfers the instructions and examples used in the prompt into training data and bakes them into the model. Pilot logs can be organized and used as a training set.
Because the learning data is memorized, performance is actually poor for new inputs. Check with a set of assessments set aside.
This is comparative data consisting of questions and standard answers. It serves as a basis for checking the extent of improvement and deciding on the next lever.

screens.outro: Now that we've seen both levers, let's establish a guideline for how to go and in what order.

ext.title: Zhou et al. (2023), LIMA: Less Is More for Alignment

screens.title: Criteria for selecting a route: in what order and to what extent
screens.lead: Select the right arrow and follow the process step by step to choose your improvement path.

steps.title: Have an assessment set and baseline
steps.body: Start with an assessment set of at least 20 questions, baseline answers, and a baseline of prompts. Without this, you won't know if any subsequent changes are for the better. Improvements that begin without a baseline are difficult to prove effective.

steps.title: Develop a causal hypothesis
steps.body: By looking at each case of error, we come up with a hypothesis about whether there was a lack of information or whether the behavior was inconsistent. The starting point is one question: “Was the input containing the facts necessary for the answer?”

steps.title: Pull the lever on the cause axis first.
steps.body: If there is a lack of information, pull the search and context lever first, and if there is behavioral inconsistency, pull the instruction, example, and tuning lever first. Levers that do not match the cause are costly and ineffective.

steps.title: Tuning starts small
steps.body: Tuning starts only when an evaluation set is available. Start small, with 50 or more good examples, and prioritize quality over quantity.

steps.title: If both are problematic, use them together.
steps.body: If both context and behavior are issues, use tuning and RAG together. Both methods are stackable, so they compensate for each other's weaknesses.

steps.title: The cost of failure determines how far you will go.
steps.body: An error that results in a refund of $1,000 when you should have refunded $100 to the customer is a completely different cost than an error in a draft that requires a human to fix. The greater the cost of one miss, the higher the aiming accuracy and the more levers are justified.

screens.outro: Now that you know the process, let's put three real-life failure cases into this flow.

screens.title: Upload 3 failure cases to the diagnosis flow
screens.lead: When you select each case, the diagnosis and prescription will unfold. First, ask yourself, “Is the information I need included in the prompt?” and then press it. Pay attention to where the prescriptions differ in each case.

items.prompt: Case A: When asked about the revised vacation regulations this year, the answer was the previous regulations.
items.answer: This is a context issue, as it requires up-to-date knowledge that is missing or out of date in the model's training data. The prompt did not contain information required for a correct answer. The solution is to search for the latest regulatory documents.

items.prompt: Case B: The answer is correct, but sometimes it is answered in a table and sometimes in a sentence.
items.answer: It's a behavioral issue because the format gets shaky while writing the same information. The information you need is already in your input. Write the format clearly as instructions, show examples of correct output, and if it still falters, consider tuning.

items.prompt: Case C: I brought related documents, but the wrong documents were mixed up, making the answer unclear.
items.answer: It's noise in the search phase, so it's a context issue. This is a case where real information is buried due to too much irrelevant context. Improved retrieval by tuning the retrieval and reducing noise is the prescription.

items.prompt: What do you see when you place the three examples side by side?
items.answer: After classification, you can see that the prescriptions are different. Cases A and C require tweaks to the search, while Case B requires tweaks to prompts and examples. If tuning had been applied to all three first, A and C would not have been resolved. Since there is only one question for classification, it can be applied in the same way even as the number of cases increases.

screens.outro: Now, with this classification, let's explain the prescriptions for the two representative symptoms.

screens.title: Commentary 1: Prescription for “the format is always wrong”
screens.lead: The instructor explains the process of diagnosing the first symptoms step by step and determining prescriptions. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: Check for symptoms
steps.body: Even if you ask the same question, the output format is different for each call, breaking the subsequent steps of receiving and processing the response. Sometimes it comes as a list, sometimes it comes as a line, so the parser doesn't work. These problems often surface as system errors rather than user complaints.

steps.title: Diagnosis: The information is already there
steps.body: In this case, the information you need is already in the input. There is nothing the model doesn't know, but the results are inconsistent, so the problem is consistency of behavior. Therefore, we need to find a prescription on the LLM optimization axis. The question required to make this judgment is: “Was the input containing the facts needed to answer it?”

steps.title: Prescription 1: Instructions and Examples
steps.body: Write the format clearly as instructions and show few-shot examples of correct output. This method is worth trying first because the preparation cost is low and the effects can be seen immediately. When you look at an example, the model mimics what the desired output should look like more accurately than when you describe it in writing.

steps.title: Prescription 2: Tuning
steps.body: If you are still wavering, collect examples of the correct format and tune it. At first, you can see results with just about 50 well-made examples. After tuning, overfitting is checked using a separate evaluation set. However, if the quality of the examples is low, the model will learn to falter, so it only selects examples that are consistently written in the correct format.

steps.title: What not to do
steps.body: Adding more searches does not improve the format. Because the lever doesn't fit the problem. Remember that adding more information and making behavior consistent are two different things. When choosing a prescription, the habit of always checking the cause axis will reduce costs.

screens.outro: Next, we will look at the prescription for the opposite symptom, “not knowing the latest information.”

screens.title: Commentary 2: The prescription for “not knowing the latest information”
screens.lead: Select and compare “If you want to solve it by tuning” and “If you want to solve it by search” alternately. Compare the two methods and consider which one is less burdensome when information changes.

states.label: If you want to inject facts with tuning
states.body: The model does not know what happened after the policy revision and answers with the previous contents. To solve this problem through tuning, let's assume that a new regulation is created as training data and trained on it. Every time a new policy comes out, the data has to be recreated and retrained. Tuning is mainly a method of learning behavior, so it is generally disadvantageous for use in adding facts. Not only is it costly and slow, but one study reported that examples containing new facts that the model did not know before learning were learned much more slowly than examples that matched known content, and actually increased the tendency to hallucinate after learning (Gekhman et al., 2024). In another study comparing methods for introducing new knowledge into a model, search methods consistently performed better than unsupervised fine-tuning (Ovadia et al., 2023). Even after learning is over, if the regulations change one more time, you will have to repeat the same thing from the beginning. Additionally, a separate evaluation is required to check whether the learned facts are accurately reflected.

states.label: When enriching context with search
states.body: If the same symptoms are not present in the model's training data or are diagnosed with outdated knowledge, it is a problem in the context optimization axis. If you use RAG, which searches for updated documents and puts them in the prompt, updating is easier than learning because you only need to update the document. After attaching a search, we separately check whether the search retrieves the correct document and whether the model uses it correctly. Maintenance becomes easier if responsibilities are divided in this way, with information updates being handled by the document side and behavioral consistency being handled by prompts and tuning. Also, keep in mind that if the document retrieved by the search is an old version, the solution is to update the document. During this process, an evaluation set is used to determine the extent of improvement.

screens.outro: Let’s summarize the reasons for the difference between the two prescriptions in one table. Check the symptoms, causes, and lever responses through the table.

ext.title: Gekhman et al. (2024), Does Fine-Tuning LLMs on New Knowledge Encourage Hallucinations?
Ovadia et al. (2023), Fine-Tuning or Retrieval? Comparing Knowledge Injection in LLMs

screens.title: Commentary 3: The reason why the two prescriptions differ in one vote
screens.lead: Read the table from top to bottom to see which causes your symptoms are connected to and which treatments lead to which treatments. It's easy to understand if you think of each row as one diagnostic case.

data.notes: For any prescription, the extent of improvement is checked with an evaluation set, and the next lever is determined based on the results. The table only provides a starting point and does not replace the answer. For example, a team that searches for issues where the format is shaky will see little improvement in the evaluation set. The results are the basis for deciding the next lever. There is not just one right answer for a symptom, and the results of the assessment set confirm the prescription.

screens.outro: In the final commentary, we will rank them in terms of cost-effectiveness.

screens.title: Commentary 4: Ordering based on cost-effectiveness
screens.lead: Move the slider to change the level of effort you put into improving. At each stage, the explanation of which lever is justified changes.

stops.body: This is the lowest preparation cost level. Start with simple prompts, clarify instructions, and add examples. This process has the side effect of creating an evaluation set and baseline, which also provides a basis for deciding whether to proceed to the next step. Without a baseline, it is impossible to know how effective subsequent improvements were.

Although it requires a search infrastructure, it directly solves the problem of up-to-date and private information. If lack of information is the primary cause of failure, this step will be most effective. We separately check the quality of the search and the utilization of the model. The advantage of search is that updating information only involves replacing documents.

Preparation takes the most time as good cases must be obtained and evaluated. Instead, it has a significant effect of increasing consistency of behavior and reducing tokens by moving instructions and examples from prompts to learning. Start only when you have an evaluation set. Costs per call can also be lowered by reducing the length of instructions written in prompts.

For tasks where both context and behavior are issues and the cost of failure is high, tuning and RAG are used together. The greater the cost of one miss, the higher the target accuracy, and the more levers are justified. The sequence is first a set of prompts and assessments, then levers aligned with the cause axis, and finally a combination of the two when needed.

screens.lead: The following flashcards illustrate the key concepts of this lesson. When you select a card, it flips over. Select the right arrow to go to the next card. After checking all cards, proceed to the next screen.

cards.back: This axis increases the accuracy of the response by adding information to the model. Pull it when you need knowledge you haven't seen in your studies, old knowledge, or private information. The representative lever is search. Example: If you are not aware of the revised vacation regulations this year.

These are the axes that make the model behave consistently in the same way. It pulls when format, tone, and reasoning procedures falter. The representative lever is tuning. Example: If the answer is correct but the format is different each time.
It is the cheapest first step on both axes. It lets you define what accuracy is and creates an evaluation set and baseline. Assessment sets of over 20 questions are created here.
This is the representative lever of the context axis. We check whether the search retrieves the correct content and whether the model uses it correctly.
Tuning is the representative lever of the action axis. The choice is based on the axis causing the failure and the cost of one failure, and if both are problems, they are combined.

screens.outro: Lastly, let's group the judgment order into one sentence.

screens.title: Decision order when encountering failure
screens.lead: The contents of this class are organized into a judgment order that can be used immediately at work. Read it slowly.

paragraphs: When performance falls short of expectations, the first thing to do is not to choose an improvement plan, but to collect examples of failures. Create an assessment set with at least 20 questions and baseline answers, and provide a baseline with prompts. That way, you can measure whether any subsequent changes are for the better.

Next, for each incorrect case, we ask, “Was the input the facts needed for the answer?” If it wasn't a context issue, go in the direction of searching and inserting information through prompts. If it was there and it was out of the ordinary, it's a behavioral issue, so go in the direction of instructions, examples, and tuning.

Tuning starts small, with at least 50 good examples, after the evaluation set is ready. If both context and behavior are issues, use tuning and RAG together. The two methods do not replace each other, but rather build upon each other.

Finally, the cost of one failure determines how much improvement can be made. An error in a draft that can be corrected by a human cannot be treated to the same degree as an error that refunds the wrong amount to a customer. For more expensive tasks, we aim higher and use more levers.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: The lever is selected according to the cause of failure. If you try to solve a problem that is wrong due to lack of information using the action lever, or if you try to solve a problem where the action is unstable using the information lever, you only end up spending money and the same failure remains.

checks.q: The model does not know the internal regulations created after learning. Which of the following correctly matches where this knowledge is missing and where it most directly fills the void?
options: There are not enough examples in the prompt, so increase the examples and change the weight.
Since this is information that has never been included in the weight, a regulation is added to the input (context) when calling.
Since the model memorized it incorrectly, the same rules are tuned repeatedly.
Context is limited, so include as much information as possible.
checks.explain: Since learned weights do not change for each call, there are no regulations in the weights after learning in the first place. The most direct way is to put the rule in context along with the question.

wrong.0: Even if an example is put into context, its weight cannot be changed. And the problem is not action, but lack of information.
wrong.2: It's not that the model memorized the rules incorrectly, but that she didn't know them from the beginning. Incorporating facts into tuning is generally disadvantageous.
wrong.3: Adding too much is not good. The necessary information must be entered appropriately, and information in the middle of a long input may be less useful.

options: Since this is a behavioral problem, increase few shots showing example output.
Since this is a behavioral issue, we start with tuning to learn the rules.
Since it's a context issue, I'll try to find the latest rules and put them in the prompt.
Since the cause cannot be determined, all three levers are applied simultaneously.
checks.explain: If the facts needed for the answer are not in the input, it is a context problem that must be solved within the context. The correct direction is to insert related information through searches or prompts, as if you were searching after opening a book.

wrong.0: Since the facts were not in the input, the cause is a lack of information, not consistency in behavior. Fewshot is a tool for teaching behavior.
wrong.1: Tuning is a lever that learns behavior, and if you try to instill facts, you have to relearn every time the rules change.
wrong.3: You can determine the cause by asking whether there were facts in the input. The lever is selected according to the axis of the cause.

checks.explain: You must have a baseline and evaluation set to check the extent of improvement, and then select a lever based on the causal hypothesis. Tuning starts small when you have an evaluation set, and works in parallel when both axes are problematic.

glossary.def: This is an axis that increases the accuracy of responses by adding information that is not in the model or up-to-date/private information through prompts and searches.
This axis increases the consistency of model behavior by making format, tone, and reasoning procedures consistent.

This method involves searching for related content and inserting it into the prompt before generating an answer. Cut the document into pieces and create embeddings (text with similar meaning changed to a list of numbers), find the fragments that are close to the question, and write them down.
A method of teaching behavior by showing several examples of correct input and output at the prompt.
Because the training data is memorized, performance is actually poor for new inputs.

The weight is the memory of the model that has been solidified through learning and is frozen at the time of learning, and the context is information that can be changed as input each time it is called.

misconceptions.myth: Tuning will also provide you with the latest information.
misconceptions.fact: Tuning is primarily a way to learn behavior. It is easier to update the most up-to-date and private information through search, and studies have also shown that adding new facts with a small amount of tuning can slow learning and increase hallucinations.

misconceptions.myth: Prompt, search, and tune are steps taken in a linear order.
misconceptions.fact: The three methods are separate levers that solve different problems. Choose the one that matches the cause of failure and write about it, and in reality, you go back and forth between the two axes by repeating evaluation, hypothesis, and application.

misconceptions.myth: After tuning, the prompt is no longer needed.
misconceptions.fact: The two stack up. Tuning is also used to shorten the tokens of long instructions and examples in the prompt.

closing.lead: The key contents of this class are summarized as follows.
points: Optimization has two axes: context (information replenishment) and action (consistency), and they solve different problems.

What the model knows comes from the weights solidified through learning and the context entered when calling, and for each failure case, it asks whether information was in the input to distinguish between a context problem and a behavioral problem.
After creating a baseline with a prompt refinement and evaluation set, you choose to search or tune.
Search targets context, tuning targets behavior, and the two can be stacked together. When writing a search, the search phase and model phase are evaluated separately.
The cost of one failure determines how much improvement can be made.
closing.reflectionLead: The questions below are for you to think about for yourself. We will not submit or grade your answers, so feel free to think about them.
closing.reflection: When you think of the one failure you see most often in your work, is it due to lack of information or faltering actions? What is the basis for that decision?
